Skip to navigation November 23, 2026 November 23, 2026 Swift SDK v4 Swift SDK v4.0.0 is the first stable release of the redesigned SDK for ElevenAgents conversations, and the core ElevenLabs library now follows semantic versioning. One ConversationClient runs any number of conversations, starting voice conversations over WebRTC with startVoiceConversation and text-only conversations over a WebSocket with startTextOnlyConversation , each with credentials matched to its transport at compile time. Client tools registered in clientTools send their own results, chatHistory updates streamed replies in place, and onDisconnect reports why a conversation ended. The v4.0.0 release notes list every change and link a migration guide from v3. Agents as code ElevenAgents agents can now be defined in code with the Agent builder in the Python and JavaScript SDKs, from v2.80.0. One definition holds the agent’s settings, its tools and its workflow, and agents.push() creates or updates the agent and every webhook and client tool it uses, filling in the tool IDs and leaving unchanged tools alone. agents.pull() and AgentProject keep agents in the same project layout as the ElevenLabs CLI, and validate() checks an agent in CI without an API key. See Agents as code . New agent LLMs ElevenAgents adds four LLMs: GPT-6.2 Sol ( gpt-6.2-sol ), GPT-6.2 Astra ( gpt-6.2-astra ), Gemini 4 Hydrogen ( gemini-4-hydrogen ) and Gemini 4 Neon ( gemini-4-neon ). Select them in the agent’s LLM picker or set them as llm through the API. The GPT-6.2 models and Gemini 4 Neon run at low reasoning effort unless the agent sets one. title: Introducing Make Endpoints
text: Introducing Make Endpoints. Release notes 2026 Introducing Make Endpoints 2 min Make Endpoints lets developers call supported app actions from JavaScript, TypeScript, or REST while keeping application logic in their own code. Use team-managed Make connections to run each action and receive its output directly. ﻿ What's new Direct app actions: Call supported app actions without creating a one-step scenario for each request. JavaScript, TypeScript, and REST support: Use generated, typed SDK clients for supported actions or call Endpoints through REST from other stacks. Managed connections: Pass a compatible Make connection ID when required. Provider credentials remain in the Make connection, not in your request input. Endpoint discovery: Check available Endpoints through team-scoped discovery and inspect SDK definitions with the `make-endpoints-cli`. Not every Make app has Endpoints, and CLI output does not confirm that a compatible team connection is available. Agent tools: Use EndpointTools to create JavaScript or TypeScript tool definitions for selected Endpoints. Endpoint logs dashboard in Make: Open the team-level Endpoint logs page to see when each call ran, which app and Endpoint it used, its status, user, connection ID, and duration. Filter the list and open Details to investigate a call. Beta pricing: Each Endpoint call costs 0.1 Make credit during beta. ﻿ Availability: Available on all Make plans, including Free. title: Working with AI
text: Working with AI. 01 Summary Related articles The AI expectations gap View more Nathan Wilmers, Maxim Massenkoff, Peter McCrory Summary How are businesses across the economy adopting AI? What bottlenecks and challenges have they faced? How can employers reorganize human expertise around increasingly capable models? To understand businesses’ experiences better, we conducted 66 interviews with 58 of Anthropic’s enterprise customers. We found: Sources of AI value. Companies are deploying AI across a dizzying range of knowledge work tasks. In particular, they are increasingly using coding agents to bring software capabilities to nontechnical roles. Interviewees report that most uses of AI add value by increasing their output, rather than by cutting costs. They attribute this both to AI accelerating existing work and to its role in introducing novel product and service improvements. Impact on employment. Across our interviews, we saw very few examples of domestic layoffs that were driven by AI automation. Although some companies reported hiring more due to AI, most companies reported hiring less due to AI. Many also reported reducing their use of contractors, particularly offshore ones. These reported cuts could be an early warning of job disruption in the international business services industry. Bottlenecks. Companies reported a range of bottlenecks, including experts resisting AI deployment and tasks that are not accelerated by AI. As coding speeds up, for example, other tasks—like code review, sales, and strategic decision-making—increasingly need to keep pace. Limits to top-down and bottom-up approaches. title: Finding faster quantum algorithms with agents and formal verification
text: Finding faster quantum algorithms with agents and formal verification. November 23, 2026 Science Finding faster quantum algorithms with agents and formal verification Sergey Shirobokov, Ben Jaderberg and Ryan Babbush Read the paper Share How using agent teams and formal verification can improve quantum algorithms for modelling fusion energy, chemistry and enzymes Quantum computers could soon solve problems beyond the reach of classical supercomputers. However, there is a catch: even when using the best quantum algorithms, some important applications still require more resources than early quantum hardware will be able to support. In a new paper , we used teams of Gemini 4 agents to improve well-known quantum algorithms, creating highly efficient quantum circuits. These optimized circuits, which are instructions for how a quantum computer should carry out an algorithm, could one day help us run simulations that solve complex scientific challenges, from fusion energy to drug design. To help the community build on this work, we are open-sourcing our Lean library , problem specifications, and verified solutions on GitHub. Because we cannot test resource-intensive quantum circuits on classical computers or today's small quantum processors, we have to prove that they work mathematically. Our agent teams proved each result using Lean, a formal theorem prover. Your browser does not support the video tag. Improving quantum algorithms using agentic teams For each problem, we tasked separate, independent agent teams with finding algorithmic improvements. These ideas were then verified with Lean, before entering a shared notebook. Every four hours, agents from each team met at a virtual conference to trade, debate and compare ideas.
